$comment: The id grammar's fixture corpus — the language-neutral half of WP1-2. Grammar: id-grammar.abnf
beside this file. Reference implementation: packages/core/src/ids.ts.
WHY A JSON FILE RATHER THAN TESTS IN THE IMPLEMENTATION'S LANGUAGE: the parser is hand-written
and a Swift/Kotlin port will be hand-written too, so nothing generates one from the other and
nothing can prove they agree by construction. These rows are the mechanism instead — every
platform's suite drives the same inputs and expectations, and a grammar change that a port has
not picked up shows up as a red suite there rather than as a wrong pixel in production. That is
the division ADR-052 decision (2) draws: generated wire shapes get equivalence for free,
hand-ported rules get it from a shared corpus.
Adding a row is cheap and is the right reflex; every `expect: null` row below is a shape some
call site used to accept silently. `why` explains rows whose expectation is not obvious — the
point of the corpus is that the *reason* travels with the case to the next platform.
Consumed by: apps/mobile/test/id-grammar.test.ts (see its header for why the TS test lives
there for now rather than in packages/core).

sampleIds.$comment: Real shapes, so the rows are not testing a fiction. KMB poles are 16 hex-ish upper-case characters, Citybus poles are zero-padded digits, GMB poles are 8 digits.

parse.name: route-kmb-plain
parse.why: The canonical four-field form. `serviceType` is a numeric-LOOKING string and must stay a string: it is an opaque operator label, and any port that decodes it as an integer loses GMB's ids and mints '1' from '01'.

parse.name: route-gmb-gtfs-id-as-service-type
parse.why: GMB route NUMBERS REPEAT across regions (there are several '1A's), so operator+number+bound is not unique for GMB. The globally unique GTFS route_id is folded into the service-type slot, where it doubles as the live-ETA route_id (ADR-047). A port that assumes the last field is small or enumerable breaks GMB.

parse.name: route-unknown-operator
parse.why: Unknown-enum tolerance (ADR-052 decision 4). The grammar validates the SHAPE of an operator code, never a closed list — the day a fifth operator ships, an already-installed client must degrade, not blank out every one of that operator's routes.

parse.name: route-reject-unknown-bound
parse.why: `bound` IS closed, unlike the operator: we mint it ourselves from the upstream I/O, so no operator can spring a third value on us. Closing it is what lets the parser return a typed direction rather than a string that is hopefully one.

parse.name: route-reject-five-fields
parse.why: The old `[, routeNo, bound] = id.split(':')` accepted this and quietly ignored the tail.

parse.name: route-reject-lowercase-operator
parse.why: Ids are minted upper-case everywhere. Accepting either case would mean two strings for one route — two cache keys, two favourites, two 'recent' entries.

parse.name: stop-ctb-leading-zeros
parse.why: The raw id keeps its leading zeros: it is the string the operator's ETA endpoint takes, never a number. A port that round-trips it through an integer requests the wrong pole.

parse.name: stop-unknown-operator
parse.why: Same unknown-operator tolerance as the route row.

parse.name: stop-reject-route-id
parse.why: THE row that pays for the exactly-two-fields rule. `split(':')[0]`/`[1]` on a route id returns 'KMB' and '6' — a plausible pole that does not exist. Shape alone must tell the two id kinds apart.

parse.name: stop-reject-place-id
parse.why: `stop.id.split(':')[0] as OperatorId` on a place id used to yield the operator 'P', which then coloured a map pin from a lookup that missed. No error, no test failure, wrong pixel.

parse.name: stop-reject-single-letter-operator
parse.why: An operator code is at least two characters precisely so that the reserved one-character place prefix 'P' can never be read as one.

parse.name: stop-reject-literal-pipe-in-raw-id
parse.why: The literal-pipe row. '|' separates the halves of a favourite key, so allowing one inside a stop id would make every favourite key ambiguous. Structural characters are rejected inside fields, not escaped — nothing in the system escapes them today, and a grammar that pretended otherwise would be describing code that does not exist.

parse.name: stop-reject-literal-plus-in-raw-id
parse.why: Same reasoning for '+', which separates place members. Note this one also survives a URL round trip badly: '+' decodes to a space in a query string, which is why place ids must be percent-encoded in a path.

parse.name: place-two-members
parse.why: The common merged kerb: a Citybus pole and a KMB pole at one stop (ADR-042).

parse.name: place-four-members
parse.why: N members, not two — a real kerb holds four poles. Every hand-written parse of this form in the app assumed a pair; a fixed-arity port would silently drop members three and four, and a place minus a member IS A DIFFERENT PLACE.

parse.name: place-single-member
parse.why: Accepted although the dataset never mints one (clustering requires two members). Rejecting it would be the grammar asserting something about the clustering rules, which are not its business — and a stale id whose siblings were retired upstream is exactly the shape a rider might have saved.

parse.name: place-reject-trailing-separator
parse.why: `.slice(2).split('+').filter(Boolean)` — the shape this replaced — dropped the empty member and resolved the id as a place of one. Silently answering with a different place is worse than answering with nothing.

parse.name: place-reject-nested-place
parse.why: Places do not nest; a member is always a pole.

parse.name: stop-or-place-pole
parse.why: /v1/stop/:id takes either shape, so the discriminated parse is what a screen actually wants.

parse.name: favourite-key-pole
parse.why: 'The 6, from THIS pole' (ADR-032). Note that BOTH halves contain ':' and the key itself contains '|' — the one id form where a naive split is not merely untidy.

parse.name: favourite-key-legacy-place-side
parse.why: The superseded scheme: keys were once written with the place id on the left, and place ids churn whenever clustering does. Recognised rather than rejected because WP2-5's migration has to FIND these to rewrite them — a parser that refused them would leave the migration nothing to work from.

parse.name: favourite-key-reject-two-pipes
parse.why: The latent bug, stated as a row. `const [stopId, routeId] = key.split('|')` returns ('KMB:AB', 'CD') here — a plausible pair, silently dropping the real route id, so a corrupt entry reads as a valid favourite for a route the rider never saved. Neither half may contain a pipe, so exactly one is required.

parse.name: favourite-key-reject-halves-swapped
parse.why: Order is part of the grammar, and each half is validated as its own kind — so a key written the wrong way round fails instead of resolving to a stop that is a route.

memberStopIds.name: members-of-four-member-place
memberStopIds.why: The shape every 'which poles do I fetch/compare?' call site wanted. Order is preserved.

memberStopIds.name: members-of-lone-pole
memberStopIds.why: A lone pole is a member set of one, so callers need no `startsWith('P:')` branch at all.

memberStopIds.name: members-of-malformed-place
memberStopIds.why: A 'P:'-prefixed string we cannot parse denotes no pole; looking it up as a literal key would be looking up a string we know is not an id.

memberStopIds.name: members-of-unrecognised-id-passthrough
memberStopIds.why: Deliberately NOT validated: anything that is not a place id is passed through as one opaque pole id and the lookup decides. This preserves what the call sites did before the parser existed, so a grammar written today cannot invalidate an id a rider saved yesterday that the dataset still resolves.

format.name: format-place-id-preserves-given-order
format.why: The formatter does NOT sort. The dataset builder sorts members by localeCompare before minting, and that ordering is baked into every published dataset and every saved favourite — re-sorting here with a different comparator would mint a different string for the same place and orphan them. Changing the collation is a migration (WP2-5), not a formatting choice.
